newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF may draw up plan for debenture holders-sources.
newsitem.headline: MOF may draw up plan for debenture holders-sources.

text.p: Japan's Finance Ministry may be forced to work out a scheme to protect bank debenture holders if Nippon Credit Bank Ltd fails to win the confidence of financial markets with its planned restructuring, banking sources said on Friday.

Nippon Credit Bank (NCB) said on Thursday that it expects to unveil a restructuring plan in early April, and banking sources said it would include the sale of real estate and the closure of some overseas operations.
"But if the markets do not like the restructuring programme, it is possible MOF will set up a framework to protect bank debenture holders," said a banking source.
The authorities may try to revise the nation's Deposit Insurance Act to protect the holders, he said.

As one of Japan's three long-term credit banks, NCB raises money mainly through issuing debentures instead of taking deposits. But the debenture holders are not protected under Japan's deposit insurance system.

The coupon rate and the yields on NCB's debentures have risen much higher recently than those for debentures issued by other banks because of fears about NCB's financial health, boosting the bank's funding costs.

Some bank officials said, however, that if the Bank of Japan (BOJ) supports NCB's restructuring plan by providing money to the bank through a fund set up to help clean up failed mortgage firms, it will help cut those costs to normal levels.
Banking sources said on Friday that the support would include the use of 80 billion yen from the fund to buy newly issued NCB shares which would then be sold to private financial institutions.
The BOJ and MOF have studied the bail-out schemes used for troubled banks in the United States and other countries, banking sources said.
Another banking official said that MOF also expects commercial banks to buy new shares to be issued by NCB in order to boost its capital.
However, it is not yet known if the commercial banks will do so, he said.

But a third banking official said he does not expect NCB to be able to restructure on its own while Japan's "Big Bang" reforms to liberalise its financial markets and boost competition are taking place.
"Sooner or later, it (NCB) may be forced to consider a merger," he said.
